Anytime I ever had the thought of doing a Pixar deep-dive, which I've been thinking about doing for a while now, the thought usually came to a halt once I remember this franchise's existence. I had the misfortune of being dragged along to see this when it was in theaters and I was in high school, and it just feeling like one of the most devastating viewing experiences of my life up to that point. Not just because it's a terrible, painfully unfunny movie with an insane premise that makes less sense the more you think about it, but because I was seeing Pixar, a film studio I respected, fully become Disney-fied, making corporate slop designed to boost merchandise profits and basically nothing else. I guess the Pixar "golden era" technically ended with Toy Story 3, but at the very least, their golden streak ended here. The main reason this was their first bust was because it has no real idea to it. "What if the world were cars" is not an idea that resonates the way their other premises did up to this point. And I really try not to be CinemaSins and just poke holes in weird premises and plots. I'm more than happy to take a fantasy at face value if it's appealing enough, or has an internal logic to it. But I cannot get behind this world at all. If this were just a zany, cartoony comedy, the dumb premise might be totally fine, discounting the fact that the jokes in this movie are painfully bad. But it's not, and quietly the worst part about this is the air of Pixar prestige it has that's in all their movies, because it dares insinuate that the "what if cars were people" movie is worthy of standing on the same pedestal. Pathetic. Well, I hear Cars 2 is supposed to be deranged, so I have that to look forward to, I guess. Can't believe this is Paul Newman's final movie, I think I need to buy a couple jars of his salsa to make this up to him.

Carros é, com folga, o trabalho mais preguiçoso, conceitualmente bizarro e cheio de fórmulas batidas de toda a história da Pixar. Em vez de entregar a genialidade emocional ou a ousadia dos grandes trabalhos do estúdio, a animação parece uma propaganda gigante para vender brinquedo de plástico, embrulhada em uma Jornada do Herói tão burocrática, previsível e sem graça que beira o insuportável. O grande erro da narrativa está na tentativa de aplicar a clássica jornada do Joseph Campbell a um protagonista raso e mimado como o Relâmpago McQueen. Ele começa como o típico babaca egocêntrico e arrogante que precisa passar por provações para se transformar, mas o roteiro conduz essa redenção de forma tão robótica que nada ali convence. Ao se perder a caminho da Califórnia e destruir a rua da esquecida Radiator Springs, McQueen é forçado a ficar preso no interior, onde encontra o batido arquétipo do mestre recluso no Doc Hudson e o alívio cômico caipira na figura do Mate — que mais irrita do que diverte. A dita "transformação espiritual" dele ao descobrir o valor da vida simples não parece fruto de uma tomada de consciência orgânica, mas sim de uma imposição das circunstâncias, fazendo com que a lição de moral no clímax da corrida final soar puramente piegas, forçando a barra para transformar um esportivo vaidoso em santo de uma hora para outra. Além dessa estrutura dramática capenga, a própria lógica do universo é um buraco negro de absurdos. É impossível se importar de verdade com um mundo feito puramente de lataria, onde a existência de portas, janelas e calçadas não faz o menor sentido pela ausência total de seres humanos. Para piorar, a direção se perde em um segundo ato extremamente arrastado, parando a história para mostrar piadas infantis de carros assustando tratores e romances sem química nenhuma entre dois automóveis. Carros pegou a estrutura mais nobre da narrativa universal e a reduziu a uma história rasa de cidade grande encontra o interior, trocando a profundidade poética da Pixar por um amontoado de clichês comerciais.

(Movie description in bold at the bottom) By the time The Incredibles (2004) came out, I was beginning to get too old for Pixar movies. I was a teenager and wanting to start enjoying more older fare. With this being said, I stopped watching a lot of Pixar films after Incredibles . Cars was the first one I didn't see, and now, on the 20 year anniversary of the films release, I feel like I really didn't miss much. Cars feels like Pixar's first real cynical movie; making a movie that feels like it was done as a vehicle (pun unintended) to sell toys first and a good movie second. This is odd considering this is the company that made the Toy Story franchise. Between world mechanics that get too confusing, and a story that just isn't interesting, Cars feels like the first real wiff in Pixar's history of great quality films. While the car mechanics can get confusing, there are aspects of the world design that are kind of nice. Examples include Sally Carrera's (Bonnie Hunt) hotel which are shaped like traffic cones (you just have to forget that this is influenced by Native American teepees) and a doctor's office being just a car mechanic shop. There are also some really nice landscapes of the American desert, which look really good. Cars are meant to take us from point A to point B. Cars asks if this go go lifestyle is really that good. It pines for the old days when experiencing life was part of living. This is done through Route 66, which traveled in a maundering way that worked with the land, instead of through it. When the interstate was built, it bypassed Radiator Springs, and car travel became simply about the destination. Cars is bringing up points that were explored in media like Fahrenheit 411 , where people travel so fast they can't see the world around them. The message of the film does work overall, and is a saving grace for the movie. The problem with the movie is the world of the Cars. As I watched the film, I got more frustrated as to what is considered a car thing and what is a take on human things. Why does Lightning McQueen (voiced by Owen Wilson) have a human-like tongue? What is Mack (voiced by John Ratzenberger) being bullied by a bunch of punk cars a parallel to in human form? Do all these cars have the life expectancy of people? By the time the movie got to the halfway point, I settled into just going with the fact that sometimes the cars are just car stuff, and the human stuff is just human stuff that the movie is doing. However, the fact that my mind was consumed with these questions as I was watching the movie is a bad sign for the movie. The cast is overall good in this movie, and it was nice to hear Paul Newman, in his last appearance in a non-documentary, but this movie does one thing that is unforgivable. It establishes a forever legacy for Larry the Cable Guy. Larry as Tow Mater is by far one of the most annoying characters ever put to screen. His southern twang and just overall annoyance was something I just never got used to. Cars 2 has the reputation of being the worst Pixar film, or at least the first truly bad Pixar film, and since it features Tow in a bigger role, I can see why. A little of Larry goes a long way, but for me I wish Larry would go far away and never come back. This movie is just boring. I really didn't care about Lightning, or any of the characters. They are all so boring and add so little. This was a movie solely meant to sell toys. I guess it worked, since this was the first non Toy Story movie to get a sequel, but for Pixar I think we all expect better than a concept that seems more fit for a Saturday morning cartoon show than a feature length film. Then again, Transformers (2007) would come out the very next year and be one of the most profitable films of that year, so what do I know? In a world populated by anthropomorphic race cars, Lightning McQueen (voiced by Owen Wilson) is one of the best race cars in the world. After finishing in a three way tie with Chick Hicks (voiced by Michael Keaton) and Strip "The King" Weathers (voiced by Richard Petty), the three cars must go to California to race in a tiebreaker. On the way west, Lightening gets lost and finds himself in the decrepit town of Radiator Springs. After damaging the towns main road, Lightening must begrudgingly repair the road as he complains and gets more annoyed with this failing town. In an alternate United States where every living thing, down to the insects (VW bugs, get it??) are living, talking cars, a new racecar tries to make a name for himself, but then gets stranded in a two bit town off route 66. I tried to watch this film when it first came out, but it was one of the dumbest things I've ever seen and turned it off after 40 minutes. One of my friends who is a big Pixar junkie later explained that these films are made for 5 year olds and his kids love them. It was interesting how even the Academy, who gives the Best Animated Feature Oscar to Pixar by default just about every single year, will barely even acknowledge this franchise (the first one was the only one even nominated but lost to Happy Feet of all things!). Anyway, it's back in theaters for the 20th anniversary and this is a really slow week for releases so I decided to finally cross it off my list for good. And yeah, it's pretty dumb. It's still Pixar so they did a decent enough job with the animation and the voice acting (and a handful of the car puns actually landed a laugh), but the content and script.... So many questions raised! Who was the Hendrix in this film? Was he a car who could play guitar, or did all the humans die out 20 years ago as Turbo Teen became a pandemic in the 80s? We have male and female cars (note how much longer the women's bathroom line is!) so are they reproducing and giving birth too? We already established that the cars age, so why don't we see any children cars? Can they drive themselves or do they ride in the back seat of their parents? What's the whole deal with cars riding in trailers of semi trucks? The truck itself is alive but the trailer isn't? So are their tires supposed to be like their shoes? And getting back to the same complaints I had when I saw F1 , what sort of stupid sport is this racing? A car gets an advantage and gets to take the lead and then they immediately send a pace car out to slow it down so that the other cars can catch up, guaranteeing that the last of 300 laps is the only one that actually matters? Worst of all, it looks like Cars 2 and 3, rather than trying to expand this weird world further, are just 2 more stories about Lightning McQueen, making me even less excited about ever 100%ing Pixar.

Wow, I was kind of underwhelmed for the most part. With nostalgic childhood movies I enjoyed as a kid, they can either really exceed my expectations because I assumed they were just fun movies without much of a good story or substance—something I would enjoy as a kid—but then I rewatch them and realize they’re actually really good, like The Karate Kid with Jaden Smith. Or, they can go the latter route and turn out more like this movie, where nostalgia was really the only thing there in the first place. And honestly, that shocked me, sadly. The opening first act was amazing with a combination of its stunning visuals and exciting race sequence. Literally couldn’t have gone any better. And then as the first act closes out, life is a highway is put on blast and you get to see those rocket league cars glow up in the night. Nothing better than that. Second act roles around and he finds himself in a town lost and strayed from his moving truck Mac and although I can appreciate the character arc he goes through in this small, charming,Humble town, much of the excitement from the first act slowly dwindles out as hes forming relationships with some of the folk in a very slow fassion, developing wholesome memories, meeting a love interest, discovering the old timer piston cup champion, most importantly, learns to be more humble, show more humility, and be less materialistic. Beyond his character development there wasn’t much redeemable here in the second act The third act race was fine and was long waited since 80% the movie took place in the old town with nothing going on! Definitely a great call and having lightning McQueen purposely lose the race to help the blue old timer finish the race one last time. Mediocre pay off as the movie in general with the invested character arc in the second act. I like how they trickled in a good bit of adult humor in a more kids advertised movie, I think there’s some great voice acting/casting with lightning McQueen, doc, Mater, and the green car. Overall, the slow second act is its weakest link and only upsides for the 2nd act is his character development and this doesn’t do quite enough for its payoff

|EN| Cars John Lasseter , 2006 Cars is one of those movies that does exactly what it sets out to do, without ever managing to leave a particularly deep impression. Lightning McQueen's story is simple and fairly classic: an arrogant protagonist completely focused on success is forced to stop and experience a world completely different from his own, eventually learning to value the people and things he used to overlook. His redemption arc is predictable, but it works. Whenever the film wants to be emotional, it actually manages to get there, especially through the relationship Lightning builds with the people of Radiator Springs. It does not try to complicate its story, and that is probably one of its strengths. The screenplay is simple, straightforward, and well written, with plenty of humor and a pace that keeps the film enjoyable. The world of Cars is also a lot of fun to spend time in. Turning a universe entirely inhabited by cars into a kind of American road movie is a simple idea, but Pixar manages to build a coherent world around it, filled with memorable and likable characters. Still, the film never left me particularly impressed. Its themes are the familiar ones of growing up, humility, friendship, and rediscovering what really matters, but they are not explored in a way that feels especially original to me. It is a good animated film, entertaining, emotional when it wants to be, and perfectly suited to the audience it was made for. But, for me, that is pretty much where it ends. Nothing wrong with it, nothing extraordinary either: a solid film, but nothing more. |IT| Cars John Lasseter , 2006 Cars è uno di quei film che fanno esattamente quello che promettono, senza però riuscire a lasciare qualcosa di particolarmente profondo. Il percorso di redenzione è prevedibile, ma funziona. Not sure why this was such a childhood staple for me, it’s good but not great. This universe does contain many unanswered questions which are more fun to ponder than actually watching the movie itself. The first racing sequence is honestly pure body horror where like 15 people die in a pile up and then lightning mcqueen breaks both of his legs and tries to drag himself across the finish line. Then he visits a tent full of rusty cars which he treats like lepers and I don’t understand what the filmmakers intention was. are we supposed to agree that rust is gross? Are these sickly, dying people? Or are they simply unwashed? My friend who is a WGA winning writer has a theory that the cars universe represents an AI/advanced alien takeover of the planet, which is then trying to re-create humanity and the human experience but with cars. I must say that I fully agree with him, and when the film is watched through this lens it becomes thoroughly horrifying and a thousand times more interesting. Like for instance, at one point a husband and wife are going on a road trip and they accidentally wind up in radiator springs, but because both of them are car people they’re taking this road trip together as two cars rather than a husband and wife together in one car. it is nonsensical and ridiculous and something that only an extremely advanced (but far removed from humanity) alien AI race in the far future could think makes any sense. Another horrifying aspect of this movie is the caste system that is inherent to the universe and which each individual is born into. If you were born as a tire changing little car thing, that is your destiny. Same as if you’re a race car, a tow truck, or a semi truck. Your career is predetermined, and there is never hope for self actualization in this society. Sally appears to belong to an elite caste, and because she’s a porsche she gets to be a lawyer, but it’s unclear if that’s directly related or if maybe luxury cars have the privilege of going to college and choosing their careers. Race cars are the gladiator caste and must subject themselves to complete disfigurement and unimaginable pain on a regular basis. Tractors are for some reason not people but instead livestock, though it’s never explained why farming is taking place. For whom is wheat being grown?? This is a good example of the AI theory. Also flies are also cars but they don’t appear to be sentient. What does it all mean???

Yes I do have quite a soft spot for this movie, I've seen it undoubtedly more times than any other movie over my entire life, and even still that doesn't make this a perfect or even great film for that matter. It carries echoes of John Lasseter's actual masterpiece, Toy Story 2 , yet stumbles through some weaker jokes and cheeky references, most of which I still have an affection for, but contrasted against 3 all-timer voice performances, this movie walks a tight line between generation-defining spectacle and reminders that this is still at its core an animated kid's movie from the 2000's. Hearing Paul Newman is the most obvious standout, bringing his classic charm to kids like me for the first time to drive home a simple yet timeless moral. Owen Wilson is a perfect other half to the main mentor/student dynamic, yet I can't shake the underlying discontent his character spends the first two acts reckoning with, especially with the context of his suicide attempt the following year. His career history of comedic roles aren't a crutch for this role, and instead the occasional vulnerability he shows makes this a surprisingly interesting undertaking for an otherwise straightforward narrative. Michael Keaton still consistently amazes me as the unforgettable asshole Chick Hicks, a role that proved to me how even Keaton's most random or commercial work has a special place in my heart existing long before I ever saw Birdman . As I get older I'll inevitably continue to love the dialogue of nostalgia and accepting change this movie presents even though the words themselves will never change, sometimes thats just what I want from cinema and this movie provides a window into my childhood like no other. Wow. I am not being hyperbolic when I say this: this is my favorite movie of all time. It has so much heart, so much depth, so many lessons, so many genuine laughs, and, yes, a couple of teary-eyed moments too. All in all, for me this really is the perfect movie. To anyone who looks down on this movie for having a fairly standard coming-of-age journey story or for it being 'just an animated kids movie,' from the bottom of my heart, fuck you. Doc and Sally are my favorite characters. Both of them have so much depth, and their voice actors both do amazingly. Paul Newman, of course, is the real star of the show. His voice just is Doc Hudson. RIP to the legend. Bonnie Hunt is a legend too. I'm just so grateful to my local theater for offering this 20th anniversary showing, because being 24 now and born just 4 years before this movie came out, I don't think I've ever gotten the opportunity to watch it on the big screen. And, what a beautiful theater experience it was. The entire time I was either smiling ear to ear, laughing out loud, or tearing up. I just love this movie. 5-year-old me did, too. Who could've guessed that that little kid would grow up to be such a film junkie, then would finally come back to Cars and feel like he's coming home. I'm so happy.
